description: We are AETHER, a 4-member team from Peru building SIGNO for the Earth System Trend Detective challenge. Our skills: Python data science, statistics, time-series and regime-change analysis (from quantitative finance), machine learning and full-stack web (FastAPI + React). We care about scientific rigor: telling real change from noise. Looking for 1 teammate with Earth science/remote sensing knowledge or design & video storytelling skills. We work remotely in English and Spanish.
summary:
SIGNO is a web app that works as a trend detective for The Amazon. It answers the central question of the challenge: is a change in a variable on Earth science real, or only a year-to-year noise?
We built SIGNO on NASA satellite data from 2001 to 2025. It tests seven measures, such as vegetation greenness, surface temperature, rainfall and tree cover in 566 squares of 1° across the Amazon. Each measure gets a Mann-Kendall trend test, a Sen slope and a correction for testing hundreds of squares at once. The map then shows which changes pass the test.
This matters because a map without that correction shows many “changes” that may be just chance. For EVI greenness, 205 squares would look significant without the correction. With it, 71 remain. A five-step guide and three demonstration cases help students, teachers and journalists read the result.
details:
1. What does it do, and how does it work?

What it does

  • Map. Pick a measure and see, square by square, where it rose or fell. Colour is the change per decade. Dotted squares have no clear trend, and hatched squares were not tested, so the reader sees at once which changes passed.
  • Area file. Click a square to see its yearly values, its trend line and the verdict for every measure there.
  • Trends. One row per measure for the whole Amazon, the Brazilian Amazon and the Peruvian Amazon: direction, change per decade with its 95 % confidence interval, and how many squares rose or fell.
  • Cross-checks. Tree cover compared between two independent datasets (Hansen and MODIS), and against fire. The rest of the interface shows one tree cover only, Hansen.
  • Method & sources. Every step, limit and dataset in plain language.
    1. The surface is heating up: daytime land surface temperature rose in 429 of 566 squares (2001–2020), and fell in none.
    2. Greenness rises in some places and falls in others: NDVI greenness fell in 48 squares and rose in 158 (2001–2020).
    3. La Pampa, Madre de Dios (gold mining): tree cover loss in this square is rising, a clear trend: the yearly loss grows by about 43.5 km² every ten years (95 % confidence interval 27.8 to 53.3).
  • Languages. English by default, and Spanish.
[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"SIGNO map of EVI greenness trends in the Amazon" ]

Figure 1. The map, here for EVI greenness: coloured squares pass the test (71 of 566) and dotted squares show no significant trend. Screenshot of the live app, 15 Nov 2026. The leaf logo in the header was generated with SI (Gemini).

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"SIGNO area file of one square" ]

Figure 2. The area file of one square: what changed between 2001 and 2025, with the yearly values of every measure. Screenshot of the live app, 15 Nov 2026.

How it works

  1. One value per year. Each year becomes one number: the mean of its 12 months (greenness, temperature) or their total (rainfall, burned area). Only complete years count, so the seasons do not enter the test.
  2. Mann-Kendall test. It asks whether the yearly values tend to go up or down more than chance explains, and gives a p-value. It only uses the order of the years, so it does not assume a straight line or normal data.
  3. Sen slope. The size of the change per decade: the median of the slopes between all pairs of years, so a few odd years barely move it. Each slope comes with a 95 % confidence interval.
  4. Many squares at once. With 566 tests per measure, some squares would look significant by chance. We apply the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate per measure, at 5 %. It limits the share of false positives among the squares that are flagged.
  5. Rules fixed before the first run. A square needs at least 80 % of its years. Greenness and daytime temperature end in 2020, because the Terra satellite's overpass time drifts in later years and the greenness anomaly coincides with that drift (r = 0.85). One rule was added after the first run: tree cover loss is tested from 2011, because Hansen reprocessed its loss data from that year on.

Architecture. A Python pipeline downloads the NASA products, clips them to the Amazon, cleans them, runs the trend test and exports small JSON files. A backend validates them against a shared data contract and publishes a read-only static API (/api/v1/). The web app reads only that API and computes no statistics in the browser, so what the map shows is exactly what the pipeline tested.

Results (run of 15 Nov 2026, evening)

Measure (years tested): squares with p < 0.05, no correction → squares that remain with the correction

Vegetation greenness, EVI (2001–2020): 205 → 71 (68 rose, 3 fell)
Vegetation greenness, NDVI (2001–2020): 295 → 206 (158 rose, 48 fell)
Rainfall (2001–2024): 115 → 69 (all fell)
Daytime surface temperature (2001–2020): 457 → 429 (all rose)

  • Temperature is the change that passes almost everywhere. Daytime land surface temperature rose in 429 of 566 squares and fell in none. The whole Amazon warmed by about 0.33 °C per decade (95 % confidence interval 0.17 to 0.55; 2001–2020, zone test).
  • Tree cover. Hansen tree cover went from 86.5 % to 77.9 % of the region between 2000 and 2025. In 2025 alone, 31,056 km² of tree cover were lost (all causes: fire, logging, mining and clearing).
  • Tree cover loss, tested from 2011. Yearly loss rose in 45 squares and fell in 2 (2011–2025). In the whole Amazon the yearly loss grew by about 12,040 km² per decade (95 % confidence interval 5,145 to 19,582). The test starts in 2011 because Hansen reprocessed its loss data from that year on, so earlier years are not measured the same way. The years 2001–2010 are shown, greyed, and not tested.
  • A known place. In La Pampa (Madre de Dios, Peru), a gold-mining area documented by independent sources (MAAP #233), the test finds tree cover loss rising: the yearly loss grows by 43.5 km² per decade (95 % confidence interval 27.8 to 53.3; 2011–2025).

2. What benefits does it have?

  • A fair answer. Students, teachers and journalists see maps of the Amazon every day, but rarely an answer to "is this change real?". SIGNO gives it, square by square.
  • Fewer false alarms. For EVI greenness, 134 of the 205 squares that would look significant do not pass the correction.
  • Easy to start. A guide of five steps and three demonstration cases. No account, no installation.
  • Open and checkable. Free, in English and Spanish, with open NASA data, open code and every step explained.
[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"SIGNO guide with three demonstration cases" ]

Figure 3. The guide for first-time visitors ends with three demonstration cases, each with a "Show this case" button. Screenshot of the live app, 15 Nov 2026.

3. What is the intended impact?

  • Who it is for: students, teachers and journalists who read or publish maps of change in the Amazon.
  • What we want to change: that people ask for the test behind every map of change, and can tell a real trend from a pattern that may be chance.
  • How far it reaches today: 566 squares of the Amazon, seven measures, up to 25 years of data, two languages.
  • Where it goes next: the project continues after the hackathon. See What comes next: our roadmap, below.

4. What tools, coding languages and software did we use?

  • Data pipeline: Python (numpy, xarray, pandas, pymannkendall, statsmodels, rasterio, earthaccess).
  • Web app: TypeScript, React, Vite and Leaflet, deployed on Vercel.
  • Data access: NASA Earthdata Login and the earthaccess library.
  • Hardware: personal computers.
  • SI tools: Claude and Gemini, as declared in Use of Super Intelligence (SI).

5. How is the project creative?

  • It shows which changes pass a test. Most maps of the Amazon show change by eye, with a slider or a before and after. SIGNO marks the squares that pass a significance test and dots the ones that do not.
  • It tests itself, in public. The app shows its own false-alarm check (shuffled years) and its own sensitivity check (a made-up trend), with the results.
  • It says what it does not know. The app explains that "no clear trend" means "not proven beyond doubt", not "nothing happened", and the limits are part of the app.
  • It teaches while it shows. The guide puts the statistical idea in one plain sentence, on the real interface.
[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"SIGNO page that explains the test and its checks" ]

Figure 4. The app explains how the test works and shows its own checks: false alarms and detection rate. Screenshot of the live app, 15 Nov 2026.

6. What factors did the team consider?

  • The seasons. Monthly data would show the calendar, not a trend. So each year is one value, and only complete years count.
  • Many tests at once. Hundreds of squares tested together produce false positives. So we correct for it.
  • The satellite itself. The Terra satellite's overpass time drifts after 2020. So greenness and temperature stop there.
  • The dataset itself. Hansen reprocessed its tree cover loss data from 2011 onward. So loss is tested from 2011 only.
  • The reader. The audience is not statisticians. So the app uses plain words, a guide and two languages.
    • A trend is a pattern in the measurements. It does not establish a cause.
    • Squares of 1° are coarse (about 12,000 km² each), and neighbouring squares are not independent. The counts of squares are not hundreds of separate confirmations.
    • The zone results (3 zones × 6 measures, 18 tests) are descriptive and not corrected for multiple tests. With a correction, 8 of the 10 clear results stay clear. The rise of tree cover loss in the whole Amazon stays clear (p = 0.0075; q = 0.017 with the correction), also with any one year left out. Loss in the Brazilian and in the Peruvian Amazon is borderline (q = 0.059 and 0.086 with the correction).
    • Hansen reprocessed its tree cover loss data from 2011 onward, and its user notes ask for care when comparing across years. So loss is tested only over 2011–2025. Hansen loss also counts canopy killed by fire, so it is not the same as official deforestation.
    • The shuffled-years check shows that the code does not invent trends from noise without memory. It does not test resistance to year-to-year memory or to similarity between neighbours.
    • The 95 % confidence intervals are published, but they are not corrected for testing many squares. For a square, the verdict is the corrected test, not the interval.
    • The comparison with NASA Giovanni is not done.
    • The Amazon boundary (RAISG biome) is provisional.
    • It does not invent trends. We shuffled the years of every square, 20 times, and ran the whole procedure again. At most 0.18 % of squares were flagged in the worst run (none for five of the six measures tested).
    • It finds a real change, but not always. A made-up trend of typical size is found in 53 to 92 % of the squares on average, depending on the measure.
    • It finds a documented place: La Pampa.
    • It stops where the satellite itself can bend a trend: greenness and temperature end in 2020.
    • Done: the data pipeline; the trend test with its correction, its 95 % confidence intervals and its four checks; the web app on real data; the guide and the three demonstration cases; English and Spanish.
    • Exploratory: the cross-checks between Hansen and MODIS tree cover and with fire (descriptive, no test).
    • Next: the four goals of the roadmap, below.

What comes next: our roadmap

SIGNO does not end with the hackathon. The code is open, every decision is written down, and the list of what comes next is public in the repository. We grouped it into four goals.

Goal 1 · Sharper science: make every verdict harder to doubt

  • Compare our trends with NASA Giovanni, as an outside check.
  • Account for neighbouring squares: publish a shuffle that keeps the patterns of the map, and correct the zone tests for multiple testing.
  • Publish the corrected value of each square next to its confidence interval.
  • Add a quality rule for clouds in the greenness data.

Goal 2 · More detail and more context

  • Go from squares of 1° to finer detail (0.05°).
  • Set the final Amazon boundary and crop the map to it.
  • Add land cover context to each square, so a reader sees what kind of place it is.

Goal 3 · Easier for everyone

  • Offer the interface language by region, and publish the data texts in Spanish too.
  • Improve the map on phones and in dark mode, and add place names.
  • Try the guide with students, teachers and journalists, and improve it with what they tell us.

Goal 4 · Open and reproducible

  • Offer quicker ways to reproduce the results, from a ten-minute check to the full run from NASA data.
  • Keep recording every method decision in the open, as we did during the hackathon.

The team: three profiles, one tool

  • Alexis · data exploration and pipeline. Explored and checked the datasets, and ran the pipeline that turns the NASA files into the numbers of the app.
  • José · prototype, web and deployment. Designed and built the interface, and keeps the live app running.
  • Kiara · pitch, documentation, communication and UX. Put the method into plain language, shaped the guide for first-time visitors, and told the story.
  • How the profiles fit together: the data feeds the tool, and the tool feeds the story. Each decision of method, design and wording was taken by the person closest to it and confirmed by the other two.

Links

  • Live app: https://signo-chi-pink.vercel.app/
  • Code repository (Apache License 2.0): https://github.com/AetherKernel/SIGNO
  • Demo video (29 seconds): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zm-PDJSuYTY
  • Explanatory slides (7 slides, PDF): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1GvY2y-yOIpuG7GOwQ4uWmOVe6L117uxv/view?usp=sharing

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. We used SI tools to speed up the work. SI did not come up with how to solve the challenge: the team chose the problem, the region, the datasets, the statistical method, its rules and the design. The whole team confirmed these decisions on 15 Nov 2026.

  • Claude (Anthropic), via Claude Code:
    • Wrote the code of the data pipeline, the trend test and the web app, to the team's specifications.
    • Wrote the documentation and the Spanish translation of the interface.
    • Drafted these submission texts and the slide deck, and wrote the code of the demo animation. The team edits and approves all of them.
    • Checked candidate data sources (existence, access, licence, citation) and reviewed the data, the trend code and the usability of the interface. The team chose the datasets.
    • Wrote the code that makes the sound of the demo video. That code cleans the recorded voice and synthesises the sound bed and the effects from sine waves and filtered noise. No sample, music library or generative audio model was used.
    • The team chose the method: the Mann-Kendall test on yearly values, the measures, the periods and the rules. Six details follow the standard choice written in the team's working kit, and the team asked Claude to apply them: the Sen slope, its 95 % confidence interval, the false discovery rate per measure, the 0.05 level, the 80 % rule and 20 shuffles.
    • The code files it wrote carry a header comment saying so.
    • Used for literature and data-source exploration.
    • Generated the team logo (a pixel-art leaf), which the team chose. It is declared here, in the repository README, on the slides and in the video.
  • The voice in the demo video is human: it is José's own voice, recorded by him. It is not generated or cloned.
  • What SI does not do: no SI model is part of the product. Whether a trend is significant comes only from the statistical test on NASA data.
  • No SI-generated content uses NASA logos or branding.
